title: Resonant LC adiabatic signaling on interposer memory wires
idea: First principles: abrupt switching burns CV^2/2 per transition no matter the driver, but adiabatic charging over time T burns only (RC/T)*CV^2. Pattern thin-film spiral inductors in the interposer RDL so each HBM lane group forms an LC tank with its own wire capacitance, ringing at the bus rate; data selects which wires join the resonant phase, and their charge returns to the tank instead of to ground.
why: Attacks data-movement energy (fact 5): with RC/T~0.05 on a 5 mm interposer wire, link energy could fall from ~3-4 pJ/bit toward ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit (5-10x).

title: Twenty-millivolt bitline-style die-to-die links bounded by kT/C
idea: The true floor on signal swing is thermal noise sqrt(kT/C), ~0.2 mV rms on a 100 fF bonded link, so 20 mV still gives >10 sigma margin. Replace 0.4 V HBM drivers with charge-dump transmitters and cross-coupled latch receivers clocked like a DRAM sense amp (precharge, share, regenerate), with per-lane offset trim stored at boot.
why: Energy ~C*VDD*dV falls ~20x versus 0.4 V swing: HBM 3-4 pJ/bit toward ~0.2 pJ/bit (fact 5), and smaller I/O cells shrink periphery (fact 7).

title: Bond sense amplifiers straight to compute and delete the PHY
idea: A bit only has to travel ~10 um vertically, so PHY, SerDes, global datapath and pads are overhead, not physics. Hybrid-bond each subarray's local sense-amp column outputs at 1 um pitch directly to registers in the logic die beneath, running millions of unserialized connections at ~200 MHz so the bitline restore charge is essentially the only signaling energy.
why: Removes global I/O wire (often >50% of read energy) and ~10-15% of periphery area; ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit HBM (30x+), bandwidth scales with area instead of shoreline (facts 5, 7).

title: Vacuum-annulus TSV liners cut via capacitance threefold
idea: TSV capacitance (~30-50 fF) is set by liner permittivity: C ~ 2*pi*eps*L/ln(r2/r1). Deposit a sacrificial carbon liner, fill Cu, then ash the carbon through vent slots to leave a sealed ~200 nm vacuum annulus (k=1) around each via, which also mechanically decouples copper expansion from silicon.
why: ~3x lower TSV CV^2 and crosstalk in HBM stacks, and the stress-free gap shrinks keep-out zones, cutting TSV area tax ~20-30% (fact 6).

title: Infrared light-through-silicon vias replace TSVs in memory stacks
idea: Silicon is transparent beyond 1.1 um, so a thinned DRAM stack is already an optical medium. Bond 1.3 um InGaAs micro-emitters on the base die that shine straight up through windowed metal stacks of 12 thinned dies; each tier has partially-absorbing Ge photodiode taps and electro-absorption shutters for the return path, forming vertical free-space buses with no holes drilled.
why: Eliminates TSV area (HBM uses ~3x DDR5 wafer area per bit) and TSV yield loss (20-30%) at ~0.5 pJ/bit, bringing HBM-class bandwidth near DDR5 cost per bit (fact 6).

title: Laserless memory dies via optical backscatter modulation
idea: The irreducible optical cost is photons, not a laser on every die. The host sends continuous-wave light into the memory package; each DRAM base die carries only ring or electro-absorption modulators with a retroreflector, encoding read data onto reflected light like RFID backscatter, so the memory side spends ~10 fJ/bit and temperature-sensitive lasers stay at the host.
why: Optical memory links at ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit over meters let DRAM leave the hot accelerator package and decouple capacity from shoreline (facts 5, 6).

title: Series voltage-stacked DRAM dies slash power-TSV current
idea: Power TSVs and bumps exist to carry current, and I^2R loss and electromigration scale with current, not power. Run four stacked dies in series from a 4.4 V rail, each floating in its own 1.1 V domain, with small switched-capacitor balancers absorbing activity mismatch, so the stack draws one quarter of the current through one quarter of the power vias.
why: Frees ~30-50% of HBM TSVs (much of the array is power/ground) for data or area savings and cuts PDN loss ~16x per via (facts 6, 5).

title: Pulse-position one-hot coding: one wire toggle carries eight bits
idea: Interconnect energy is paid per transition, not per bit. On wide hybrid-bond buses where wires are cheap, send each byte by toggling exactly one of 256 wires (position = value), or 1 of 16 wires in 1 of 16 time slots; edge-detecting receivers decode. Random NRZ spends ~4 transitions per byte, this spends 1.
why: ~4x fewer charge events per bit on die-to-die links (fact 5); multiplies with low-swing gains.

title: Single-flux-quantum superconducting interposer for cryogenic memory links
idea: An SFQ pulse costs Ic*Phi0 ~ 2e-19 J, about 10^4 below CMOS link energy. For 4 K cryo-AI and quantum-control systems, route memory traffic on passive niobium microstrip lines in the interposer that carry SFQ pulses ballistically without dispersion, with CMOS-to-SFQ converters at the cryo-DRAM edge.
why: aJ-scale data movement with zero resistive loss, and cryo-DRAM needs almost no refresh (facts 5, 3).

title: Active interposer sums partial results while data travels
idea: Bits that will be added together should never travel separately. Make the interposer an active 28 nm die with reduction trees at routing junctions between HBM stacks and compute tiles, so all-reduce, gradient accumulation and partial-sum merging happen inside the wire and only reduced results reach the GPU.
why: Cuts memory-to-compute traffic in reduction-heavy phases by the stack count (~4-8x) and its pJ (fact 5).

title: Diamond interleaf wafers make DRAM-on-logic thermally survivable
idea: The shortest data path is DRAM directly on logic, but heat raises leakage and refresh rate. Bond 30 um polycrystalline CVD diamond wafers (k ~1500 W/mK) between logic and DRAM tiers with laser-drilled Cu vias, spreading hotspots sideways before they reach the cells.
why: Lets DRAM sit ~50 um from compute (~0.1 pJ/bit vs 3-4) while holding cells <=85 C so refresh does not double (facts 5, 3).

title: Five-micron DRAM tiers with bitline-pitch nano-TSVs
idea: TSV diameter is set by copper fill aspect ratio (~10:1) times die thickness, so the TSV tax is really a thickness tax. Thin each DRAM wafer to 5 um on a temporary carrier and stack wafer-on-wafer, allowing 0.5 um vias at ~1 um pitch tucked into subarray gaps instead of a dedicated TSV region.
why: Removes most of HBM's ~3x area-per-bit penalty and keep-out zones while raising vertical bandwidth ~100x (fact 6).

title: Uncut DRAM wafer serves as the interposer for chiplets
idea: An interposer is just wires on silicon, and a DRAM wafer is already silicon with metal. Leave the DRAM wafer uncut, add a top RDL, and hybrid-bond logic chiplets face-down so each sits on its own memory field; boot-time self-test maps out bad dies and routes around them through the wafer RDL.
why: Deletes interposer, dicing, KGD handling and HBM TSVs: wafer-scale bandwidth at <0.2 pJ/bit and ~30-40% lower packaged cost per bit for HBM-class memory (facts 5, 6).

title: Twin synchronized predictors send only the surprise
idea: Information theory says only unpredicted bits must cross a channel. Run identical stride/context/value predictors on both sides of the memory link; the sender transmits a 1-bit hit flag when the receiver's prediction is right and an XOR residual otherwise, and both update identically so they stay in lockstep.
why: Regular pointers, zeros and strides could cut bits crossing the interface 2-5x, lowering link pJ and bandwidth demand (facts 5, 8).

title: ESD-free die-to-die pads via laser-cut sacrificial shorting ring
idea: ESD diodes often contribute over half of an I/O pad's capacitance, yet they only matter during handling. Tie all bond pads to a metal shorting ring through dicing and stacking, then laser-ablate or fuse the ring after bonding, leaving bare pads at ~1-2 fF instead of ~100 fF.
why: 2-4x lower CV^2 per bit on chiplet and HBM links and smaller I/O area (facts 5, 7).

title: Molybdenum CTE-matched TSVs: no keep-out zone, no tungsten
idea: Keep-out zones exist because copper (17 ppm/K) fights silicon (2.6 ppm/K). Fill TSVs with CVD/ALD molybdenum (4.8 ppm/K) so thermal stress drops ~5x, allowing transistors right next to vias and avoiding tungsten, which China supplies at ~80%.
why: Shrinks TSV area overhead ~30-50% and removes a chokepoint metal from the stack (fact 6, resources).

title: Spare-die HBM stacks with base-die crossbar remapping
idea: Stack yield compounds as y^N, so 12 dies at 98% bond yield gives ~78%. Build 13-high stacks whose base die holds a channel crossbar that remaps any failed die to the spare, plus spare TSV lanes rerouted at runtime without fuses.
why: Turns compounding yield into binomial 12-of-13 yield, recovering most of HBM's 20-30% yield loss for ~8% extra silicon (fact 6).

title: Terahertz in-package broadcast: one transmission feeds every chiplet
idea: A wire costs energy per destination; a radiated wave costs once for N receivers. Put 300 GHz on-chip antennas on the HBM base die and every compute chiplet inside a metal-lidded package cavity acting as a waveguide, broadcasting weights or shared activations to all chiplets simultaneously.
why: For multi-chiplet weight broadcast, energy per delivered bit falls ~N (4-16x) versus point-to-point copies (fact 5).

title: CCD bucket-brigade memory where moving data is storing it
idea: A CCD keeps charge packets with no contact or transistor per bit and moves them by clock phases, so the cell is only gates (~4F^2) and access is the movement itself. Build circulating CCD loops in depreciated image-sensor fabs with a regenerating sense stage per loop, holding 3-4 bits per packet thanks to few-electron read noise.
why: Dense, contactless, low-mask streaming memory tier without EUV or capacitor etch (facts 1, 4, 7); trades random-access latency.

title: Logic-die wordline segment drivers kill 128x page overfetch
idea: Overfetch exists because global wordlines are long and drivers are costly in DRAM process. Hybrid-bond a logic die whose fine-pitch bonds drive each 512-cell local wordline segment directly, so a 64 B read activates 64 B of cells instead of an 8 KB row.
why: Cuts random-read energy from ~5.9 pJ per useful bit toward ~0.2 pJ (fact 8) and shrinks row-hammer aggressor exposure (fact 9).

title: Photon-counting avalanche receivers near the 20-photon quantum limit
idea: A shot-noise-limited receiver needs only ~20 photons per bit for 1e-12 BER, while PIN+TIA links burn ~10^4 because of amplifier noise. Use Ge-on-Si avalanche/SPAD arrays with pulse-position modulation, where each photon pulse carries log2(M) bits, so the laser budget falls by orders of magnitude.
why: Optical memory links at ~0.1 pJ/bit or less, making far-memory DRAM energy-competitive with HBM (fact 5).

title: Air-bridged interposer wires: vacuum dielectric cuts wire capacitance
idea: Wire capacitance per mm scales with permittivity, so oxide or polyimide (k 3-4) costs 3-4x the energy of vacuum. Build RDL lines over a sacrificial polymer and release it, leaving lines suspended on periodic posts in a sealed cavity like MEMS air bridges.
why: ~3x lower CV^2 for every interposer and chiplet bit, and faster lines allow lower swing (fact 5).

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory pods with kT-scaled link swings
idea: Thermal noise and leakage both scale with temperature: at 77 K, kT drops 4x, copper resistivity ~7x and access-transistor leakage collapses. Immerse HBM-plus-accelerator modules in LN2 and redesign links for ~4x lower swing, longer unrepeated wires and lower threshold voltages, with refresh nearly eliminated.
why: ~2-4x link energy reduction plus refresh removal and a lower voltage floor (facts 3, 5, 10).

title: One optical copy of weights broadcast to a hundred accelerators
idea: First principles: read-only weights need O(1) storage, not O(N) copies, if broadcast bandwidth exists. Keep one model copy in a central memory node and stream it in layer order through a passive 1:128 optical splitter tree to accelerators running in lockstep; each holds only a few-layer SRAM ring buffer.
why: Weight GB per accelerator falls ~100x, so cost per served GB ~100x lower; trades scheduling flexibility (all nodes run the same layer at once).

title: Time-share each DRAM gigabyte among a hundred tenants via optical swap
idea: A working set only needs DRAM while it runs. Give accelerators small DRAM plus a co-packaged-optics swap path (~10 TB/s) to a NAND pool and gang-schedule jobs so each job's working set swaps in for a 10-20 ms slot; one DRAM GB serves ~100 tenants in rotation.
why: Effective DRAM per tenant ~100x lower; trades latency, job slicing and swap energy.

title: Little's-law deep-queue byte interface over cheap NAND
idea: Bandwidth = bytes in flight / latency, so a 20 us medium delivers 1 TB/s if 20 MB are in flight. A controller chiplet beside the GPU exposes load/store addresses over SLC NAND with a 64k-entry tagged queue and 64 B read reassembly, while GPU warps hide the latency and an SRAM log absorbs writes.
why: Working memory at NAND cost (~100-200x cheaper per GB than 2026 DRAM); trades latency and write endurance.

title: Compiler-scheduled deterministic streaming replaces random access
idea: Transformer inference has a static access order per layer, so cache misses are a choice. The compiler emits a cycle-exact fetch schedule, and a stream engine pulls tensors from QLC NAND exactly one schedule-window ahead into a 64 MB SRAM; DRAM holds only what the compiler cannot predict.
why: Removes DRAM for static tensors (often >90% of bytes); cost per GB tracks NAND (~100x cheaper); trades generality to static-graph workloads.

title: Flash-on-logic hybrid bonding reads 100,000 planes in parallel
idea: NAND bandwidth is limited by narrow package pins, not the array: each plane senses 16 KB per ~20 us. Hybrid-bond a 3D NAND array wafer face-to-face with a compute wafer so 10^5 planes each get their own bonded bus, giving ~80 TB/s from a medium priced like flash.
why: HBM-class bandwidth at ~100x lower cost per GB for read-mostly weights; trades write endurance and 20 us latency.

title: Circulating drum memory: streaming access refreshes ultra-leaky cheap cells
idea: Capacitor size and leakage specs exist only to hold charge for 64 ms; if every row is read-and-restored every 100 us because data circulates through compute like a drum, retention can be 640x worse. That permits planar MIM capacitors on short bitlines and leaky access devices in fully depreciated 28-40 nm fabs, with no high-AR etch and no EUV, behind a controller that streams rows in fixed order.
why: Strips capital (~55% of wafer cost) and the capacitor/EUV steps; claimed 10-100x lower cost per GB with high uncertainty; trades random access for sequential revolution latency.

title: Nanoimprinted oxide-TFT memory built into glass package substrates
idea: Display fabs process glass at ~$100-300/m^2 versus ~$70,000/m^2 for finished DRAM wafers, a ~300x area-cost gap. Use nanoimprint lithography at 40-50 nm half-pitch on Gen-8 panels to pattern oxide-TFT gain cells, then cut the panel into glass-core package substrates carrying the memory directly under the chiplets.
why: At ~1/3 DRAM density, cost per bit ~100x lower and U.S.-manufacturable in display/glass lines; trades speed, retention and density.

title: Compressed-sensing readout makes selector-less crossbars usable
idea: The cheapest possible cell is a two-terminal resistor at a wire crossing with no transistor or selector, but sneak paths forbid single-cell reads. Read a whole 1k x 1k tile with pseudo-random row voltage patterns, measure column currents, and let a decoder in the interface chiplet solve the linear system (with sparse coding and block parity) to recover every bit.
why: 8-16 stacked BEOL crossbar layers at 4F^2 with 2-3 masks each could approach ~100x cheaper per GB; trades latency (us tile decode), energy and endurance.

title: Seeded procedural weights regenerated beside the multiply units
idea: A tensor's true storage cost is its Kolmogorov complexity, not its size. Train models whose matrices are W = PRNG(seed per block) times a few learned coefficients, and place LFSR/hash generators next to the MAC arrays to regenerate weights on the fly, so memory holds seeds and coefficients only.
why: 10-100x fewer stored and moved bytes, so cost per effective GB ~100x lower; trades training effort and some accuracy.

title: Mandated e-waste DRAM harvest re-hosted behind CXL adapter chiplets
idea: Millions of working DDR4 DIMMs from retired servers are shredded yearly, and their manufacturing cost is already sunk. A procurement/ITAD rule requires federally funded and hyperscale decommissions to route DIMMs to re-hosting, where a CXL card with a protocol-translation chiplet, strong ECC and per-chip retirement masks pools 32-64 old DIMMs as a far-memory tier.
why: Bits cost only test plus adapter (~$0.05-0.2/GB), ~50-100x below 2026 contract DRAM; trades energy, density and bandwidth; supply bounded by decommission flow.

title: Content-addressed memory fabric stores each identical page once
idea: Across a datacenter, KV-cache prefixes, system prompts, libraries and weights repeat thousands of times. A CXL switch hashes 4 KB pages on write, keeps each unique page once in a pooled DRAM/NAND backend, and hands hosts copy-on-write pointers, with a prefix-trie index for KV caches.
why: Shared-prefix chat serving can dedup 10-100x, so effective cost per served GB ~100x lower; trades write latency and isolation complexity.

title: Idle chat sessions keep tokens, not KV caches, until resumed
idea: A KV entry is ~100-500 KB per token but the token that produced it is 2 bytes, and most KV memory belongs to sessions idle between user turns. Evict idle sessions to token IDs only and re-prefill them on return using cheap older-node recompute chiplets, trading FLOPs for bytes.
why: Resident KV memory falls 100x+ for typical chat duty cycles; trades resume latency and prefill energy.

title: Read-only charge-trap chiplets programmed once at wafer sort
idea: A deployed model's weights never change, and storage with no write path is the cheapest physics allows. Program 3D charge-trap arrays with weights at wafer sort via massively parallel probe cards, then ship dies with the program/erase pumps stripped, thicker retention oxide, and read-in-place sensing bonded beside compute.
why: Bit cost at or below 3D NAND (~100x+ cheaper than DRAM) with smaller periphery; trades flexibility (new model means new chips).

title: Spatially pipelined chiplet mesh: activations never land in memory
idea: Intermediate buffers exist only because producer and consumer run at different times. Map each layer group onto its own chiplet in a panel-scale mesh and chain them with FIFOs sized to pipeline skew, so activations flow directly chiplet to chiplet and activation DRAM goes to near zero.
why: Activation memory falls >100x; trades reconfigurability and needs many chiplets.

title: Lookahead router streams mixture-of-experts weights from flash
idea: Only ~3-6% of MoE experts fire per token, and later layers' routing can be predicted from the current hidden state. A tiny lookahead router predicts layer l+2 experts and triggers flash fetches two layers early, so only the active expert slice lives in DRAM and the rest sits on NAND.
why: Expert-weight DRAM drops ~20-50x; blended with NAND at ~1% of DRAM price, cost per GB ~50-100x lower; trades misprediction stalls.

title: Volume holographic page memory steered by silicon-photonic phased arrays
idea: A hologram stores a megabit page per angle in a cheap photopolymer block and reads it in one flash onto a detector array, so bandwidth comes from page parallelism, not fast cells. Replace slow angle addressing with silicon-photonic optical phased arrays switching in ~100 ns, and hybrid-bond the detector array to an SRAM page buffer.
why: Medium cost could make read-mostly working sets ~100x cheaper per GB; trades write speed, latency and alignment robustness.

title: Layer-major execution turns all memory traffic into hard-drive streams
idea: Weight bytes per token equal W/B for batch B, and random access disappears if you run one layer over an entire corpus before the next. For offline workloads (embedding, synthetic data, evaluation), stream weights and the corpus's activations layer by layer from striped HDD/NAND arrays, with DRAM only as small staging.
why: Working storage at HDD/NAND cost ($0.015-0.05/GB, >100x cheaper); trades latency completely (hours-scale jobs).

title: Learned activation codecs inside the memory interface die
idea: Activations lie on low-dimensional manifolds, carrying far less information than 16 bits x width. Put a per-layer trained transform plus vector quantizer and entropy coder in the HBM/CXL base die so tensors are stored as 8-16x smaller codes and expanded on read, with error budgets set by training loss.
why: 10-30x effective capacity alone and ~100x when codes live on a NAND tier; trades accuracy and codec latency.

title: Compute embeddings from hashes instead of storing terabyte tables
idea: Recommendation embedding tables are terabytes of mostly cold rows hit by random gathers. Replace lookup with deep-hash embedding: k hashes of the ID feed a small on-accelerator MLP that synthesizes the vector, while only the hottest ~1% of IDs stay in an explicit cache.
why: Table memory falls 100-1000x and random-gather traffic disappears; trades compute and some accuracy.

title: Fab-reject partial-good DRAM dies stitched by remapping base die
idea: Dies that fail one bank, speed bin or retention test are scrapped even though >90% of their cells work. Buy them at scrap price, stack 8-16 on a cheap logic base die that self-tests at boot and remaps at 1 KB granularity around bad regions, and sell the result as a slower seconds-grade memory tier.
why: Die cost near zero, package plus base die ~$0.1-0.3/GB, ~30-100x below 2026 contract DRAM; trades speed and density; supply ~5-10% of output.

title: Delta-merge-on-read lets thousands of fine-tunes share one base
idea: A fine-tuned model differs from its base by a low-rank delta under 1% of parameters. A delta-merge unit in the memory base die applies each tenant's LoRA or sparse delta as base weights stream out, so 100+ tenants each appear to own a full model while memory holds one base plus tiny deltas.
why: Memory per served model ~100x lower; trades a few % quality versus full fine-tunes and adds base-die compute.

title: Decoupled access chiplet runs the address stream microseconds ahead
idea: Latency hurts only when addresses are known late, and most programs compute addresses from a small slice of their code. Compile that address slice onto a tiny access-processor chiplet that runs ~10 us ahead of the main core, issuing loads to a slow SLC-NAND or far-memory tier so data lands in a queue just in time.
why: Hides microsecond latency for irregular but computable access (graphs, sparse), so media at ~1% of DRAM price acts as working memory; trades slip penalties on data-dependent branches.

title: Address-event storage keeps only coordinates of nonzero values
idea: When activations are >99% zero (ReLU-fied LLMs, spiking nets, event sensors), storing the zeros wastes ~99% of bits. Store tensors as address-event streams (index plus small value) in the interface die, expand them only inside SRAM next to the MAC arrays, and train with sparsity regularizers targeting 99%+.
why: Bytes stored and moved fall 30-100x for sparse tensors; trades model architecture freedom.
